title: Too Late to Love Me
excerpt: After years of being overlooked by her husband, Claire discovers that leaving him may be the only way to reclaim her life.

sections.title: Prologue
paragraphs: For the first time, his eyes were red.
His voice, usually so calm and controlled, had gone hoarse.
"I married you first. I was the one who made you fall in love with me." His fingers tightened around hers. "You were supposed to stay with me for the rest of your life."
He stared at her as though sheer desperation could change what had already happened.
The silence between them stretched on until even breathing seemed unbearably loud.
There was no anger in it anymore. No grief, either.
It sounded almost like a sigh.

sections.title: Chapter One
paragraphs: Everyone in the capital knew about the wedding of Prince Adrian Vale and Lady Claire Ashford.
For weeks, it was all anyone could talk about.

The royal boulevard had been covered in flowers. White roses climbed the iron gates of the cathedral, while carriages bearing the crests of the kingdom's oldest noble families filled the streets from one end of the capital to the other.
Thousands had gathered simply to catch a glimpse of the bride.
When Claire stepped from her carriage in an ivory gown embroidered with pearls, people said she looked exactly as a future queen ought to look.
The young ladies of the capital had nearly driven themselves mad with envy.
After all, Claire had not merely married a wealthy duke or some decorated military commander.
She had married Prince Adrian Vale.
A man with royal blood, considerable influence, and a very real chance of someday inheriting the throne.
More importantly, no one could claim that Claire was undeserving of such a marriage.
House Ashford was one of the most powerful military families in the kingdom.

For generations, the Ashfords had commanded armies along the northern border. Claire's father and older brothers had all distinguished themselves in battle, crushing rebellions, defending the frontier, and uncovering conspiracies before they could threaten the Crown.
Her father, General Edmund Ashford, was practically a legend.

When he was still a young officer, he had ridden alone through enemy lines to rescue the king during a disastrous campaign. He returned half-dead, his armor soaked in blood and one eye permanently blinded.
From that day forward, House Ashford possessed something far more valuable than land or gold.
They possessed the king's absolute trust.
So when the time came to choose a bride for Prince Adrian, there had been little serious competition.
Claire Ashford was the obvious choice.
If she had been plain, foolish, or spoiled, perhaps the other noblewomen might have comforted themselves by whispering that Adrian had married her only for her family.
Unfortunately for them, Claire was none of those things.

She was beautiful in a quiet, refined way. She had received the finest education available to a noblewoman and could discuss history, literature, politics, and estate affairs without embarrassing herself. She played the piano beautifully, spoke three languages, and possessed the kind of flawless manners that made elderly duchesses adore her.
Since childhood, other daughters had been compared to her.
Why couldn't you sit like Lady Claire?
Why couldn't you speak as gracefully as Lady Claire?
Why couldn't you behave like an Ashford?
She had spent her entire life becoming the sort of woman no one could criticize.
Claire had known him since childhood.
Their families were close. They had attended the same royal gatherings, spent summers on neighboring estates, and grown up within the same glittering circle of aristocratic families.
To outsiders, their marriage seemed almost inevitable.
A prince and the daughter of the kingdom's most powerful general.
Childhood companions becoming husband and wife.
Royal blood joined with military power.
It was the sort of love story people enjoyed believing in.
Everyone agreed that Claire Ashford had been given a perfect marriage.
Because Claire knew exactly how little the beautiful wedding had meant.

She knew what remained after the cathedral emptied, after the bells stopped ringing, after the guests drank their final glasses of champagne and the last carriage disappeared through the palace gates.
She knew what waited beneath all that perfection.
A single cold laugh from her new husband.
Claire had been nervous that night.
She had loved Adrian for years.
Perhaps she had loved him for so long that she could no longer remember exactly when it had begun.
That morning, her attendants had started preparing her before sunrise.
Her hair had taken hours. Tiny pearls had been woven between carefully arranged curls, and the weight of her veil had made her neck ache before she even reached the cathedral.
Claire had walked down the long cathedral aisle with her back perfectly straight.
She had stood before hundreds of nobles without stumbling over a single word of her vows.
She had smiled when she was supposed to smile.
Curtsied when she was supposed to curtsy.
Danced when she was expected to dance.
Not once had she allowed the exhaustion to show.
By midnight, the celebration had finally ended.
One by one, the servants withdrew from the royal apartments.
The heavy doors closed behind them.
And for the first time that entire day, Claire was alone with her husband.
Her heart began to beat faster.
She sat at the edge of the bed, hands folded carefully in her lap.
For years she had imagined this moment in embarrassing detail.
She had wondered what Adrian would say when they were finally alone.
Would he finally look at her not as the girl who had followed him around as a child, but as a woman?
The thought made warmth rise into her cheeks.
Adrian was standing several feet away from her, loosening the collar of his formal coat. The tenderness she had secretly hoped to see was nowhere in his expression.
"Enough," he said. "You can stop pretending now."
Claire's fingers tightened in the fabric of her gown.
She wasn't sure she had heard him correctly.
"Don't you find this whole performance exhausting?"
For a moment, Claire couldn't speak.
The words landed harder than they should have.
Years of discipline came to her rescue.
Whatever she felt, she did not show it.
She steadied herself and raised her eyes to her husband.
"It's been a long day," she said gently. "Perhaps we should have some wine and—"
Adrian's expression darkened before she could finish.
"Haven't you performed enough for one day?"
"This marriage wasn't something either of us chose," he continued. "We played our parts for the court. The ceremony is over. There's no audience anymore, Claire."
He gave her a humorless smile.
The last sentence drained the color from her face.
Was that what he thought this was?
She had married him only hours ago.
Was expecting her husband to remain with her on their wedding night already asking too much?
Apparently, her silence irritated him even more.
"I wasn't going to be cruel to you," he said. "We've known each other since we were children. Whatever else has happened, I did care about you."
"You're like a younger sister to me. You always have been."
"We could have remained that way. We could have grown up, married other people, and lived perfectly happy lives."
The accusation she had been waiting for without realizing it.
He continued before she could answer.
"You knew how I felt about her. Everyone close to me knew."
"And yet you let your family use its influence with my father to force this marriage through."
"You got what you wanted," Adrian said bitterly. "Congratulations."
Each sentence seemed to cut a little deeper than the one before it.
That she had never asked her father to pressure the king?
That when the royal marriage proposal arrived, she had been just as shocked as Adrian?
Looking at his face, Claire already knew the answer.
And the more she refused to defend herself, the more certain Adrian became that he had been right all along.
He had known for years that Claire loved him.
She had never said it aloud, but as a girl she had been terrible at hiding it.
Her eyes always found him first in a crowded ballroom.
Whenever he returned from riding or hunting, she somehow appeared nearby.
If he mentioned liking a particular book, she would have read it by the next time they met.
If he praised a piece of music, she would secretly learn it on the piano.
When they were children, her affection had been painfully obvious.
And Adrian had never known what to do with it.
Because to him, Claire had always been Claire.
The well-behaved girl who followed him through palace gardens.
The general's daughter his mother insisted he include whenever the royal children played together.
His heart had belonged to someone else long before Claire became his bride.
It belonged to the first girl who had ever made him forget what was expected of a prince.
The girl whose laughter had filled one summer afternoon with sunlight.
The girl who wore scarlet when every other young lady chose pale silk and pearls.
The girl who laughed too loudly, spoke too freely, and never seemed frightened of him simply because he was royal.
The girl who had occupied his thoughts for ten years.

sections.title: Chapter Two
paragraphs: Claire adjusted to married life with remarkable speed.
Within days, she had taken control of nearly every matter concerning Adrian's household.

Major financial decisions, correspondence with noble families, the hiring and dismissal of servants, invitations, gifts, household accounts—even trivial disputes among the staff eventually found their way to Claire.

She remembered the names of senior servants after meeting them only once. She knew which merchants had been overcharging the household, which tenants were behind on their rents, which horses needed replacing, and which members of the staff had relatives serving in influential households elsewhere in the capital.
By the end of the first month, the prince's residence ran more smoothly than it had in years.
No one could find fault with its new mistress.
When Claire was summoned to the royal palace shortly after the wedding, she spent half the afternoon in the Queen's private sitting room.

She had chosen her gifts carefully: imported perfume for the Queen, a first edition of a book she knew the older woman enjoyed, and a small silver music box commissioned from one of the finest craftsmen in the capital.
Nothing extravagant enough to seem calculating.
Nothing careless enough to suggest indifference.
Claire had always been good at exactly right.
For nearly two hours, they spoke about estate affairs, upcoming receptions, the charities Claire would now be expected to patronize, and the duties that came with being a royal wife.
The Queen lifted her teacup and studied Claire over its rim.
Claire's fingers paused for the smallest fraction of a second.
A faint blush appeared across her cheeks.
The Queen's expression softened almost immediately.
She didn't need Claire to say anything.
The Queen leaned back against the upholstered chair.
"I know these matters are embarrassing when one is newly married. But I am a woman before I am your queen, Claire. I worry."
"If you can give Adrian a child soon, preferably a son, your position will become considerably more secure."
The Queen reached across the small table and brushed a loose strand of hair away from Claire's temple.
There was genuine affection in the gesture.
Claire had known her since childhood.
The Queen had watched her grow from a solemn little girl into the woman sitting before her now.
"I have always thought of you almost as a daughter, so I hope you will listen to me carefully."
"If Adrian ever becomes involved with another woman, don't make a scandal of it."
That made them no easier to hear.

"Men in his position are rarely permitted simple lives. There will always be women around him. Some because they admire him, some because their families want influence, and some because Adrian himself may choose them."
"You are his wife. You are Princess Adrian Vale. There will be hundreds of people watching you, waiting for the smallest mistake."
Claire looked into the Queen's eyes.
For one reckless moment, the truth rose all the way to her lips.
He left our room on our wedding night.
The Queen released a breath as though Claire's answer had lifted some enormous burden from her shoulders.
She leaned back, suddenly looking tired.
"You were always such a sensible child."
The Queen closed her eyes for a moment.
"I think I need to rest. You should go home."
A lady-in-waiting escorted Claire through the palace.
They passed marble galleries, long corridors lined with portraits of dead kings, and enormous windows overlooking the autumn gardens.
Claire maintained her posture until she was inside her carriage.
Until the palace gates closed behind her.
Until there was no one left to see.
Then something inside her gave way.
Her chest tightened so painfully that she struggled to breathe.
Tears gathered in her eyes, blurring the carriage window and turning the capital outside into shapeless patches of gray and gold.
Claire pressed her handkerchief beneath one eye.
She wiped the tears away before they could fall far enough to ruin her makeup.
Even alone, she couldn't quite allow herself to cry properly.
That shouldn't have hurt as much as it did.
She had known before the wedding that he didn't love her.
She had known all of it.
But knowing something and living through it were very different things.
He had walked out on her wedding night.
He hadn't even cared who saw him leave.
Had Claire's personal maid, Anna, not been the only servant stationed outside the bedchamber, rumors might already have spread throughout the capital.
The king certainly seemed to have heard something.
The morning after the wedding, Claire and Adrian had gone to the palace together for the customary family audience.
Partway through the visit, the king had ordered Adrian into his study alone.
Claire never learned exactly what was said.
But whatever happened behind that closed door had left Adrian furious.
By the time Claire returned to their residence later that afternoon, Adrian had already locked himself inside his study.
One of the footmen quietly informed her that His Highness had returned from the palace pale with rage.
And, apparently, one rather expensive chair.
She merely instructed the kitchen to prepare dinner.
Then she sent trays to his study several times throughout the evening, ensuring enough servants saw her do it.
Later, she ordered every lamp in the corridor outside Adrian's study to remain lit until morning.
And then she retired to her own room.
Instead, Claire sat at her desk until sunrise, writing letters to churches and charitable organizations in the southern provinces.
By the next morning, Anna had casually mentioned to several members of the household that the prince had been deeply troubled by reports of catastrophic flooding in the south.
Government relief funds had mysteriously disappeared into the hands of corrupt officials.
His Highness, she explained, had been so distressed by the suffering of his people that he'd remained awake all night in his study, examining reports and searching for ways to help.
Her mistress, equally moved, had spent the night arranging charitable donations and offering prayers for the victims.
It took less than a day for the story to leave the household.
Within three days, half the capital had heard it.
By the end of the week, the story had become almost heroic.
Prince Adrian, unable to sleep because of the suffering of ordinary citizens.
Princess Claire keeping vigil beside him.
A young royal couple united in compassion and duty.
Some newspapers even compared him favorably with the Crown Prince.
Claire knew Adrian understood exactly what she'd done.
She had taken the humiliation of their wedding night and the destruction of his study and transformed both into political capital.
More importantly, she had improved it.
At times, she suspected he genuinely despised her.
But he wasn't foolish enough to destroy a useful lie simply because she'd created it.
Because Adrian possessed an ambition far stronger than his resentment toward his wife.
And Claire knew how to help him acquire it.
His political advisers seized the opportunity almost immediately.
Donations were sent south in Adrian's name.
His allies arranged for newspapers to cover every shipment.
At the same time, damaging stories began appearing about officials associated with the Crown Prince's faction.
Whether the timing was accidental, no one bothered to ask.
For several weeks, Prince Adrian Vale became the capital's favorite royal.
She never asked for his gratitude.
Then, one month after their wedding, another announcement shook the circles of high society.
Lady Evelyn Hart was getting married.
Evelyn was the youngest daughter of an old aristocratic family.
Her engagement was to Nathaniel Brooks, a brilliant young lawyer whose sudden rise in government had made him one of the most talked-about men of the season.
The wedding was to take place at the end of the month.
Claire learned about it three days before Adrian mentioned it.
Not that he ever actually mentioned it.
But she saw the change in him.
Spent longer hours away from home.
Several times, Claire noticed him staring at nothing for minutes at a time, his expression dark and distant.
On the night of Evelyn's wedding, Adrian disappeared.
It was Anna who came quietly into Claire's private garden to tell her.
Claire looked up from the book resting in her lap.
"The stable boy believes one of the horses is missing, but he isn't certain when it was taken."
Claire was silent for a moment.
"His Highness is working privately tonight and does not wish to be disturbed."
"No threats," Claire added. "Give them something instead."
Claire remained beneath the flowering tree in the garden.
Small white petals drifted down every time the wind passed through the branches, collecting across the table, her skirt, and the dark surface of her untouched tea.
Claire sat there for a long time.
Long enough for the tea to turn completely cold.
So that was why Adrian had destroyed his study after meeting with the king.
He had learned about Evelyn's engagement.
The king must have told him deliberately.
Perhaps he had hoped the news would finally force his son to accept reality.
Whatever had existed between them was over.
Kings were accustomed to sensible solutions.
Claire tightened her fingers around the porcelain cup.
Perhaps Adrian had gone to see Evelyn.
Perhaps he was watching her wedding from a distance.
Perhaps he intended to speak to her before she belonged permanently to another man.
What mattered was whether anyone had seen him leave.
What mattered was whether rumors would spread.
What mattered was whether his enemies could use tonight against him.
It was a rule Claire had learned so young that sometimes it felt more instinctive than breathing.
Don't give anyone something they can use against you.
Her fingers gradually relaxed around the cup.
A flower petal landed on the back of her hand.
Then her gaze moved toward the small clock visible through the open garden doors.
She had been so occupied with Adrian, with Evelyn's wedding, with making sure the servants kept quiet—
Today was supposed to have been her birthday.

sections.title: Chapter Three
paragraphs: Claire Ashford had been born beneath an unlucky star.
At least, that was what her parents had been told.

When Claire was only a few weeks old, her mother had invited a celebrated astrologer to the Ashford estate. The woman was famous among the aristocracy for reading birth charts with unsettling accuracy, and Lady Ashford—anxious after years of failed pregnancies before finally giving birth to a daughter—had wanted nothing more than reassurance.
The astrologer studied the infant's chart for a long time.
Then she quietly announced that the child had been born under a deeply unfortunate alignment.
And, should she grow reckless, the possibility of violence and an early death.
General Ashford had nearly thrown the woman out of the house.
She had been wanted so desperately and loved before she was even born. To hear, only weeks after finally holding her in their arms, that her life might be marked by suffering was unbearable.
The astrologer eventually offered them a solution.
The girl's true birth date should be kept private.
Public records would list another day—one associated with prosperity and good fortune.
More importantly, Claire was to be raised carefully.
She should be taught restraint, discipline, scholarship, and impeccable conduct.
Perhaps, the woman said, fate could not be defeated.
Claire's parents accepted the advice with almost desperate gratitude.
And so Claire's childhood became a collection of rules.
Don't do anything that might invite danger.
Her mother employed the strictest governess she could find.
If Claire held her fork incorrectly, she was corrected.
If her posture slipped, she was corrected.
If she spoke too quickly, laughed too loudly, or displayed too much temper, she was corrected again.
As a child, Claire never understood why.
She only knew that her brothers were allowed to come home muddy and bruised from riding while she was scolded for running through a corridor.
She knew that they learned fencing while she learned embroidery.
That they climbed trees while she watched from beneath them.
That they could disappear into the woods for hours while Claire was expected to remain indoors with a book.
Until one summer afternoon, when obedience became unbearable.
There was a festival in the capital that day.
Music floated across the streets. Merchants had set up colorful stalls beneath striped awnings, selling sugared almonds, ribbons, toys, cakes, and tiny glass ornaments that caught the sunlight.
Claire could hear the noise from inside the family's townhouse.
It remained one of the brightest memories of her childhood.
Musicians played in the square while children chased one another between stalls. Bright banners snapped overhead. There was cinnamon in the air and fresh bread and flowers and horses.
Claire wandered through it all with enormous eyes.
No one reminding her to walk slowly.
For perhaps an hour, she experienced the extraordinary pleasure of being an ordinary child.
Years later, she would pass through those same streets countless times.
They never looked as beautiful again.
She was standing near a confectioner's stall when a hand suddenly seized her arm.
A broad woman in a worn cloak dragged her away from the crowd.
"There you are!" the stranger snapped loudly. "How many times have I told you not to run away from your mother?"
The woman's fingers dug painfully into her arm.
Her voice disappeared beneath the noise of the market.
Claire stumbled after her, frightened tears gathering in her eyes.
Then someone caught her other hand.
A boy stood on her other side.
He couldn't have been much older than she was.
His coat was expensive, his boots polished, and there was an effortless confidence in his expression that Claire had never seen in another child.
The boy looked Claire up and down with exaggerated thoughtfulness.
Then he looked at the stranger.
"Because she looks clean, well-fed, and nothing like you."
"I think you're trying to steal her."
She never managed to bring it down.
Three men appeared almost instantly from the crowd.
Another forced her arm behind her back.
The third stepped between the woman and the children.
It happened so quickly that Claire simply stared.
Only later did she understand that they had been royal guards traveling in plain clothes.
And only later still did she discover the identity of the boy who had saved her.
At the Ashford gates, he turned to her with an amused little smile.
Then he climbed into his carriage and disappeared down the road.
Claire stood at the gate staring after him long after the carriage was gone.
What followed was considerably less romantic.
The moment Claire returned, Lady Ashford seized her, cried over her, scolded her, and punished her so severely that Claire herself began sobbing.
It was the first time she had ever seen her elegant, composed mother completely lose control.
"Do you understand me? You could have disappeared and we might never have found you."
Claire had never heard her sound so frightened.
Eventually, terrified by the possibility that her mother truly hated her, Claire threw her arms around her waist and begged forgiveness.
Mother and daughter ended up crying together.
That night, Lady Ashford finally told Claire the truth.
About the false birthday recorded in public documents.
Claire was too young to understand most of it.
But she remembered one thing very clearly.
Her real birthday was a secret.
Something ominous enough that everyone around her had decided it was safer to pretend it did not exist.
As Claire grew older, she stopped resenting her parents.
Eventually, she even came to understand them.
They hadn't wanted to imprison her.
And perhaps they had been right.
Being controlled, measured, proper—perhaps all of it had protected her.
So Claire learned to accept it.
And years later, on the night of her real birthday, she sat alone beneath the flowering trees in her garden and guarded a cup of tea that had long since gone cold.
Before she could rise, two arms suddenly closed around her from behind.
The sharp smell of alcohol surrounded her.
She hadn't heard him enter the garden.
She hadn't even known he'd returned.
For one absurd moment, Claire's first thought was not *Where have you been?*
Who saw you come home like this?
She was already calculating which servants might need to be spoken to in the morning when Adrian rested his chin near her shoulder.
His voice was lazy with drink.
It was an expensive white tea imported from the southern coast.
"If you would like some, I'll have Anna prepare a fresh pot. This one has gone cold, and drinking it may—"
Adrian picked up the pot before she could finish.
Tea spilled from the corner of his mouth and splashed onto her shoulder.
Cold dampness spread through the fabric of her dress.
"Cold tea for someone who arrived too late."
He dropped the empty pot onto the grass.
Then, without warning, he lifted Claire into his arms.
Her hands immediately caught around his shoulders.
He carried her toward the house.
Not because she understood what he intended.
But because the last thing she wanted was servants appearing to investigate the noise.
Even now, she was thinking about appearances.
Inside her bedchamber, Adrian lowered her onto the mattress.
His movements were clumsy with alcohol.
For several seconds he simply stood over her.
"What do you actually want from me?"
There was something raw in his expression that frightened her more than anger would have.

"You are one of the king's most capable sons. House Ashford has defended the kingdom for generations. A marriage between our families strengthens the Crown and demonstrates my family's loyalty. In the future—"
The blow came before she could finish.
Claire's head snapped to the side.
For a second, everything was silent.
Perhaps, drunk as he was, he had not realized his own strength.
Perhaps he had not meant to hit her so hard.
Heat spread violently across Claire's cheek.
Slowly, she turned her face back toward him.
His anger, suppressed all night, finally broke.
"You people tore us apart and you don't even care!"
Claire's fingers curled into the sheets.
"Do you have any idea what tonight is?"
"The woman I love belongs to another man now."
He looked at Claire as though she were personally responsible for every miserable choice that had brought him to that room.
"I'll never be her husband. I'll never wake up beside her. I'll never have the life I wanted."
"And you stand there talking about loyalty and the Crown as though I'm nothing but a piece on someone's chessboard."
Something inside her became very quiet.
The rest of that night passed in pain and confusion.
Adrian's grief became cruelty, and Claire—trapped between shock, fear, and the lifelong instinct never to cause a scene—endured what followed without calling for help.
She stared upward at the dark canopy above the bed.
A tear slipped from the corner of her eye and disappeared into her hair.
She remembered Adrian at nine years old, standing in a crowded market and refusing to let a stranger take her away.
She remembered meeting him again at a royal dinner months later.
They had spotted each other across the long table.
Claire had nearly forgotten how to breathe.
Later, when she trusted him enough, she told him her secret.
She had expected him to laugh.
Or worse—to look at her the way superstitious people sometimes looked at things they considered cursed.
Instead, several days later, on the date no one else acknowledged, Adrian found her in the palace gardens.
He pushed a small box into her hands.
Inside was a silver pendant shaped like apple blossoms.
"I don't care what some ridiculous astrologer said."
He spoke with all the certainty only a child could possess.
Claire clutched the little pendant in her palm.
"Look around you. It's spring. Everything's blooming. How could a day like this possibly be cursed?"
At that age, he had seemed made of sunlight.
Claire had fallen in love with that boy long before she understood what love was.
Not long afterward, the same shining boy had found her again with an excited expression.
He leaned close, as though sharing the greatest secret in the world.
Her heart had stopped for the first time.
Claire could still remember every detail of his face.
Every note of happiness in his voice.
"When I grow up, I'm going to marry her."
And that night, across the capital, Evelyn Hart became Nathaniel Brooks's wife.
While in another house, Claire Ashford finally became Adrian Vale's.
And not in any way the girl she had once been would have dreamed of.

sections.title: Chapter Four
paragraphs: For months afterward, Claire and Adrian barely spoke.
Fortunately, the kingdom provided them with a convenient excuse.
The floods in the south had worsened.
Whole districts needed reconstruction, and the king appointed Adrian to oversee the royal response.
Adrian threw himself into the work.
He traveled constantly, inspecting damaged towns, supervising the repair of bridges and levees, investigating officials accused of stealing relief funds, and meeting local authorities.
While Adrian dealt with the disaster itself, Claire managed the story surrounding it.
She appeared at churches and shelters.
She arranged temporary housing for refugees who reached the capital.
She opened one of the family's warehouses as a distribution center for food and blankets.
Every effort was made in Adrian's name.
Together—though rarely in the same place—they became an extraordinarily effective political partnership.
Claire made sure the kingdom saw him working.
By the end of the crisis, the floods had been brought under control and several corrupt officials arrested.
The king publicly praised Adrian's leadership.
Soon afterward, he granted his son a dukedom and greater authority over several provinces.
Prince Adrian Vale became the Duke of Westbridge.
His influence at court grew dramatically.
Months after leaving, Adrian finally returned to the capital.
He had only intended to stop at the residence long enough to collect several books and documents before another meeting.
Instead, he turned a corner and almost walked directly into Claire.
For a married couple, they looked remarkably like strangers.
There had always been something delicate about Claire, but now the bones at her wrists seemed sharper and her face more fragile.
His eyes moved, almost unwillingly, to her cheek.
Nothing to prove what had happened.
And he remembered waking the following morning with enough fragments of the night remaining to understand exactly how cruel he had been.
He had fled the room like a coward.
What disturbed him most was not the guilt he felt toward Evelyn.
For ten years, Adrian had believed his devotion to her proved something noble about him.
He had loved one woman faithfully.
Even after losing her, he had convinced himself that remaining untouched by anyone else was some grand testament to that love.
Yet when that ended, he discovered something deeply uncomfortable.
He wasn't thinking about betraying Evelyn.
About the look on her face.
About what he had done to her.
About how she had not screamed at him afterward.
That silence had followed him south.
Fortunately, royal orders had arrived almost immediately, giving him an excuse to leave the capital.
He traveled until exhaustion made sleep unavoidable.
He filled every hour with meetings, inspections, reports, and arguments.
Still, news from home reached him.
He heard that Claire had been skipping meals while organizing relief efforts.
A week later, he quietly ordered expensive tonics and supplements sent back to the estate without his name attached.
He heard that she had begun visiting refugee camps outside the capital.
He immediately assigned additional guards to the area.
Officially, they were there to protect the supply convoys.
Unofficially, every one of them had orders to keep Claire safe.
He told himself it was guilt.
After all, she was his wife.
Whatever he thought of their marriage, harm coming to Claire would create a political disaster.
Yet standing across from her now, Adrian suddenly had no idea what to say.
He had spent months imagining this moment.
Sometimes he thought he would apologize.
Other times he imagined pretending nothing had happened.
His title had changed, and Claire had changed with it immediately.
"Do you need anything for the household?"
Claire apparently decided to rescue him from it.
"The Queen is hosting the Spring Assembly next month."
"Attendance is optional, but ambassadors from the Kingdom of Arden will be present. Her Majesty intends it as a diplomatic reception, so I believe your presence would be beneficial."
"The marriage office has sent over profiles from several noble families."
Claire continued in the same composed voice.
"I reviewed them and selected several women whose families, education, and character would make them suitable."
"I thought you should make the final choice yourself."
He stared at her as though she'd insulted him.
"We haven't even been married a year."
"And you're already trying to put another woman in my bed?"
"I suppose I gave you too much credit. I thought House Ashford cared about appearances."
Claire folded her hands neatly before her.

"While you were away, I made certain that every important family in the capital heard about your work in the south. House Ashford publicly supported your relief program, and the reputation you've acquired is strong enough that taking a companion now would do little damage."
"The women I selected come from respectable families. Each is educated, discreet, and socially acceptable."
Her tone might have been used to discuss hiring a secretary.
"Because the arrangements would be made with my approval, no one could credibly portray the matter as a scandal. On the contrary, it would suggest harmony within your household."
Claire did not seem to notice.
"People already know that you value intelligence in those around you. Selecting an educated woman would only strengthen the image that you care about merit rather than ornament."
"And if your wife herself approves, no one can accuse you of humiliating her."
Adrian couldn't find a single weakness in it.
And for some reason that infuriated him.
One phrase repeated inside his head.
Some trace of the girl who used to follow him through palace gardens with her entire heart written plainly across her face.
A mask polished so carefully that he couldn't find the woman underneath it.
Her head remained politely lowered, as though she were simply waiting for him to leave.
Adrian had planned this reunion differently.
During the long months away, he had imagined speaking to her calmly.
Instead, when he leaned closer, the words that came out were bitter.
"You really can't wait to put someone else in my bed, can you?"
From the other end of the corridor, any servant watching them might have mistaken the scene for intimacy between husband and wife.
Only Claire heard the anger in his whisper.
"You think all of this is clever."
His mouth was close to her ear.
"The perfect wife. The perfect household. The perfect political strategy."
Then he turned and walked away.
His footsteps disappeared down the corridor.
Her fingers were clenched so tightly around the fabric of her skirt that her knuckles had turned white.
For one brief, irrational moment, Adrian had expected her to stop him.
Anything would have been better than that immaculate silence.
But Claire Ashford did none of those things.
She simply stood there and watched her husband leave.
And Adrian found, to his irritation, that her indifference bothered him far more than her love ever had.

sections.title: Chapter Five
paragraphs: In the end, Adrian chose one woman from the profiles Claire had prepared for him.

She came from a minor noble family with little political influence. She was educated, played the piano well, understood poetry, and possessed all the polished accomplishments expected of a respectable young woman.
But Claire knew immediately why Adrian had chosen her.
Lily looked remarkably like Evelyn Hart.
The resemblance was impossible to miss.
The shape of her face, her eyes, even the way her dark hair framed her features—under soft candlelight, the similarities became almost unsettling.
Adrian's thoughts were painfully easy to read.
Claire closed the jewelry case in front of her and drew a slow breath.
She gripped the edge of the table until the dizziness passed.
Her health had been poor lately. She tired easily, and if she remained standing for too long, black spots sometimes appeared at the edge of her vision.
Anna immediately reached for her arm.
She had never liked calling Claire *Your Highness* after the wedding, and she liked her new title as Duchess of Westbridge even less.
Claire saw her maid turn away, blinking rapidly.
"Do you think I enjoy correcting you?"
"There are people watching everything that happens in this house."
"They watch what I say, what I wear, who visits me, how often His Grace comes to my rooms. They'll watch you too."
"If you give them something to gossip about, they'll use it."
Anna had served her since childhood.
Perhaps that was why the girl still remembered a version of Claire that no longer seemed to exist.
The girl who could sometimes laugh without first wondering who might hear.
Anna had watched that girl disappear beneath layer after layer of responsibility.
And what hurt her most was that Claire never complained.
No matter how deeply she was wounded, her back remained straight.
Lily Bennett arrived at Westbridge House several days later.
To Claire's surprise, Adrian did not behave as she had expected.
He spent the first evening with Lily, but afterward he rarely visited her apartments. Government affairs provided an easy excuse, and he began spending more and more nights away from home.
When Lily came to formally introduce herself to Claire the following morning, disappointment was obvious on the younger woman's face.
Nothing had happened between Lily and Adrian.
That realization produced a feeling Claire refused to examine.
She accepted the tea Lily offered her.
After several minutes of polite conversation, Lily hesitated.
"I've heard His Grace is very busy."
"If you ever find yourself lonely, Your Grace, I would be happy to keep you company."
"I play the piano. I read quite a lot as well. We could play together, or perhaps discuss books."
Claire's fingers paused against the rim of her cup.
"I can see how devoted the two of you are to one another."
Claire nearly wondered if she'd misheard.
What on earth had Adrian told this woman?
Perhaps the illusion Claire had worked so hard to create had become convincing enough that even someone living beneath the same roof believed it.
Claire had no intention of correcting her.
"You needn't worry about your future. You'll be well provided for here."
No promises she might later regret.
Words, Claire had learned, were dangerous precisely because they could not be taken back.
Over the following days, Adrian returned home several times.
He visited neither Lily nor Claire.
If they didn't see each other, they couldn't quarrel.
Unfortunately, two people living in the same house could not avoid each other forever.
Several days later, Claire prepared to visit St. Aurelia's Abbey.
No formal procession. No elaborate entourage.
She had nearly reached her carriage when she encountered Adrian.
Claire lowered her eyes and waited for him to dismiss her.
Instead, after several seconds, Adrian said, "I'll come with you."
She couldn't hide her surprise quickly enough.
Adrian seemed almost equally surprised by his own words.
But he had already spoken them.
Then he walked toward the carriage.
Claire remained still for a moment before following.
At the carriage door, Adrian turned and offered her his hand.
His palm was broad and warm, roughened by years of riding and sword practice.
Once, long ago, that hand had reached for hers in a crowded market.
She remembered being a frightened little girl and believing that as long as Adrian held her hand, nothing terrible could happen.
She climbed into the carriage quickly and withdrew her hand at once.
Adrian remained outside for half a second longer.
Then he climbed in after her without saying anything.

sections.title: Chapter Six
paragraphs: The journey to St. Aurelia's passed mostly in silence.
Claire rested against the carriage wall with her eyes closed.
He didn't know why he'd offered to accompany her.
The words had simply come out.
Perhaps it was because one of his aides had spent half the previous evening reporting everything Claire had done for him while he was away.
The political alliances she'd quietly strengthened.
Or perhaps it was something simpler.
Perhaps Adrian was finally beginning to understand that Claire was his wife.
Evelyn had been married for more than half a year now.
A life that no longer included Adrian.
He couldn't spend the rest of his own life worshipping a memory.
Even asleep—or pretending to sleep—she looked guarded.
Her hands rested neatly in her lap.
There was no softness in her posture.
Did this woman ever truly relax?
Evelyn had never been like that.
Evelyn laughed when she was happy and shouted when she was angry. She ran through gardens, climbed fences, said whatever came into her head.
She was alive in a way Claire never seemed to be.
And yet that same maddening self-control was exactly why she managed his household so well.
Why she protected him so effectively.
Why every crisis became smaller the moment Claire involved herself.
When they arrived at St. Aurelia's, Adrian stepped from the carriage and walked away without offering his hand again.
The abbey stood several miles outside the capital, surrounded by old trees and rolling hills.
Its stone buildings were centuries old, the halls cool even in summer.
A young novice escorted Claire and Adrian into a private receiving room.
Claire and Adrian were alone again.
Claire looked toward the narrow stained-glass window.
Then, almost despite himself, he smiled faintly.
He had stopped speaking like a duke.
It had happened so many years ago that Claire had assumed he might have forgotten.
Then she realized how foolish that thought was.
Of course Adrian remembered this place.
This was where he had met Evelyn.
Adrian's expression softened as the memory returned.
One of Adrian's guards entered hurriedly and whispered something into his ear.
He rose and followed the man out.
Adrian had brought her to the abbey when they were children because he'd heard there was an enormous stray cat living in the woods nearby.
He had decided they were going to catch it.
Adrian constructed a ridiculous trap from rope, branches, and food stolen from the abbey kitchens.
While they waited, he climbed trees, threw stones into the river, picked wildflowers, and chased insects.
She remembered watching him with shining eyes.
Eventually, something moved near the trap.
They had not caught a cat.
A furious little girl covered in leaves and dirt.
The girl struggled against the rope.
"Then your trap isn't very good, is it?"
"Let me out," the girl demanded. "I want to see whether this ridiculous thing can actually catch anything."
The first time Adrian saw her, she was trapped in a net and laughing at him.
And somehow, from that moment onward, his attention never quite returned to the quiet girl standing behind him.
Claire remembered that afternoon now almost as though it had happened to someone else.
And Claire standing a few feet away.
She couldn't even remember what happened to herself afterward.
Had her mother scolded her for wandering too far?
Had her legs hurt from walking?
"You don't have to be so formal."
Claire lowered herself back into the chair.
"I haven't been feeling well lately. I'm sure it's nothing serious."
"Small troubles have a habit of becoming serious ones when ignored."
The priest looked at her for a long moment.
"You've spent your life holding on very tightly."
"Eventually, the person you hurt most by refusing to let go is yourself."
"But perhaps it's time you considered showing yourself the mercy you so freely give everyone else."
"What exactly are you still holding on to, Claire?"
What was she holding on to?
The promise she'd made to her father?
The belief that if she endured long enough, behaved well enough, loved quietly enough, one day everything would become worthwhile?
After the door closed, the old man remained seated.
He looked down at his tea.
"So many years since I read that child's stars."
A weary sadness crossed his face.

sections.title: Chapter Seven
paragraphs: Claire returned to Westbridge House alone.
Adrian never came back to the abbey.
She waited in the carriage for more than an hour before finally telling the driver to leave.
She didn't ask where Adrian had gone.
Several days later, the Queen summoned Claire to the palace.
The message claimed Her Majesty had been feeling unwell and wanted company.
Claire suspected there was more to it.
The Queen was reclining beside an open window when Claire entered.
"No curtsying today," she said. "Come sit with me."
Claire turned the question back politely.
"There's very little left for me to do in this palace. I hardly have enough work to exhaust myself."
"You don't need to speak to me as though we're in court."
"Your father and I knew each other quite well when we were younger."
Claire looked at her in surprise.
Her father had never mentioned that.
Before she could ask, the Queen said quietly:
The Queen gave a soft, skeptical sound.
One by one, the women left.
When the doors finally closed, she reached for Claire's hand.
"He isn't cruel by nature. But that boy has always had difficulty understanding what he truly wants until he's already lost it."
"His reputation among the ministers has risen dramatically. In some circles, he's now more popular than the Crown Prince."
"That is part of why the king granted him Westbridge so quickly."
"There are things I cannot discuss openly, even with you."
Then she whispered something into Claire's ear.
Much later, when she left the palace and the gates closed behind her, she remained silent in the carriage.
She stared through the window without seeing the streets.
For the first time in months, she desperately missed her mother.
She missed waking in the morning without a household full of people waiting for her decisions.
She missed being someone's daughter instead of someone's wife.
Claire had known what road she was choosing.
Or at least, she should have known.
Especially after the conversation she'd once had with her father.
Now she had to live with it.
When Claire returned home, she discovered Adrian waiting in her apartments.
That was unusual enough to make her stop.
She started to greet him formally.
Adrian clearly wanted to say something.
He simply refused to say it.
Claire quietly served him food while he ate with the expression of a man arguing with himself.
Eventually dessert was cleared and tea brought in.
"The Queen hasn't been feeling well. I kept her company."
"The Spring Assembly is in a few days. The delegation from Arden is definitely attending?"
Claire finally set down her cup.
"Is there something you want to ask me?"
"My father intends to send someone south."
"There have been attacks along the border. General Whitmore has been ordered to suppress them."
"I want command of the royal contingent."
The irony was impossible to ignore.
This was the man who had accused her of using House Ashford's influence to force him into marriage.
Now he was asking her to use that same influence for him.
"If General Ashford recommends me to the king, I'll have a strong chance of receiving the appointment."
"I'm sorry, but I can't ask my father to do that."
For several seconds, he seemed genuinely unable to understand her.
Some part of him still believed Claire owed him this.
That House Ashford's power was now his by marriage.
"The Crown Prince's supporters are already watching you. The Crown Prince himself has made no serious mistake, which means the king currently has no reason to reconsider the succession."
"If you continue pushing yourself forward, you risk two things."
"First, you'll make the Crown Prince see you as an immediate threat."
"Second—and more importantly—you may make the king see you as one."
"You married an Ashford. Everyone already assumes my family's military influence supports you."

"My father and brothers command soldiers. General Whitmore commands soldiers. If you suddenly obtain a military appointment that places you close to another powerful commander, what do you think your father will see?"
A prince building an army around himself.
"So you think I should do nothing?"
"I think you should let someone else take this opportunity."
"You solved the southern flood crisis. That was civil administration. This is different."
That sentence landed harder than she intended.
Several of his advisers had warned him about exactly this.
Others had insisted the opportunity was too valuable to surrender.
They had appealed to his pride.
His fear that another prince might gain what he refused.
Now that Claire had stripped away the emotion, the danger seemed obvious.
Someone among his advisers was either dangerously incompetent—
or deliberately encouraging him toward reckless decisions.
For the first time, he felt something close to fear when he considered what might have happened had he followed the wrong advice.
Why had his first reaction to Claire's refusal been rage?
Why had he immediately wanted to wound her?
He remembered the cruel things he'd said before.
Things that would have devastated almost anyone.
And Claire had endured them all.
Adrian looked at his wife differently.
And she had just protected him from himself.
Why shouldn't he try to accept that?
She gave him a small smile.
Candlelight traced the pale line of her throat.
She knew immediately what he wanted.
She made the movement subtle enough that it could almost be mistaken for nothing.
"I'm afraid I'm not feeling well tonight."
"I'll have the kitchen send something warm in the morning."
Claire escorted him to the door.
She watched him disappear into the dark corridor.
Only then did she release the breath she'd been holding.
That first night had left something behind.
Her body remembered before her mind could reason with it.
Hadn't she decided long ago that marrying Adrian meant accepting whatever came with him?
But wanting to become someone's wife did not mean wanting to be hurt.
Claire had never demanded that Adrian love her.
She knew his heart had belonged to Evelyn.
If circumstances had been different, perhaps Adrian and Evelyn would have married.
Perhaps they would have been happy.
She had wanted something much smaller.
Claire had never been someone who demanded more once she'd been given enough.
She understood the importance of knowing when to stop.

sections.title: Chapter Eight
paragraphs: By the night of the Spring Assembly, the atmosphere between Claire and Adrian had changed.
Nothing between them was ever dramatic anymore.
But Adrian began joining her for dinner.
Sometimes he remained afterward in the small library, reading correspondence while Claire worked at her desk.
They could spend an entire hour in the same room without speaking.
During one of her visits, she covered a smile with her hand.
"His Grace seems to be spending quite a lot of time here lately."
Lily's smile suggested she believed nothing of the sort.
Weren't many marriages built on less?
Claire prepared carefully for the Spring Assembly.
Her gown was elegant without being extravagant, a deep blue silk with silver embroidery.
Too plain, and people would whisper that Adrian neglected his wife.
Too elaborate, and she risked appearing desperate for attention.
She and Adrian arrived at the palace together.
At first, the evening proceeded perfectly.
Claire joined several noblewomen while Adrian spoke with ministers elsewhere in the ballroom.
Then a familiar voice came from behind her.
Evelyn Hart—now Evelyn Brooks—was walking toward her.
Marriage had changed her title but little else.
She wore a vivid crimson gown, her dark hair swept elegantly upward, yet somehow she still possessed the same bright energy Claire remembered from childhood.
She looked like sunlight walking into a room.
She reached automatically for Claire's arm.
The smile on Evelyn's face faltered.
One of them smiled behind her fan.
"Oh, Claire and I have known each other since we were girls. She knows I hate all these ridiculous formalities."
Once, Claire might have envied that.
Perhaps part of her still did.
But this was no childhood garden.
"It would be better not to address me so casually here."
Something wounded appeared in Evelyn's eyes.
One of the older women waited until Evelyn was out of hearing before laughing softly.
"Spirited is one word for it," another replied.
"Imagine calling the Duchess of Westbridge by her first name in the middle of a royal reception."
She merely smiled faintly and lifted her glass.
Once, Adrian would have seen Evelyn's wounded expression and immediately gone after her.
At least, Claire thought he wasn't.
Guests returned to their assigned places as the formal portion of the evening began.
Claire sat beside Adrian near the royal table.
His gaze kept drifting toward the lower tables.
When Evelyn had been absent from his life, perhaps it had been easier for Adrian to convince himself he'd moved on.
Old feelings were rarely considerate enough to remain buried.
A herald announced the arrival of the foreign delegation.
Representatives from the Kingdom of Arden entered the hall.
Their leader approached the king and bowed before presenting a ceremonial gift.
He was tall and broad-shouldered, dressed in black formalwear edged with gold embroidery. His clothing was noticeably different from the fashions of Valeria, severe in cut but exceptionally elegant.
A mouth that seemed permanently on the verge of an amused smile.
But his eyes were what caught Claire's attention.
Eye colors that light were rare in Valeria.
Claire looked a second too long.
Their eyes met across the hall.
But not before she saw his smile deepen.
And for the first time that evening, someone other than Adrian Vale was watching Claire Ashford.

sections.title: Chapter Nine
paragraphs: By the time the banquet began to wind down, Adrian had drunk enough to loosen his restraint, though not enough to lose control entirely.
Claire noticed the difference almost immediately.
His attention kept drifting toward the lower tables.
At first, the glances were brief.
Claire wasn't angry because he was looking at another woman.
At least, that was what she told herself.
What troubled her was that other people might notice.

They were seated close to the Crown Prince and several of the most politically observant nobles in the kingdom. A careless expression, a glance held half a second too long—sometimes that was all a court needed to create a scandal.
Across from them sat the foreign ambassador Claire had noticed earlier.
She learned his identity only after he came to offer Adrian a ceremonial toast.
"This is a spirit from Arden," he said.
Claire reached automatically for her own glass.
Before she could drink, the ambassador gave a small cough.
"In Arden, women are under no obligation to drink at formal dinners. I doubt anyone here would consider it discourteous if the Duchess declined."
Then his gaze shifted toward Adrian.
"Surely her husband would be willing to finish it for her."
Adrian barely seemed to think about it.
He took Claire's glass and drank both portions.
When the man moved on to the next table, Claire leaned slightly toward her husband.
"He doesn't seem like an ordinary diplomat."
"He's Prince Julian Arden. The second son of their king."
Claire glanced toward the foreign prince again.
Especially the eyes that seemed to smile even when his mouth did not.
Near the end of the reception, Evelyn left her table.
Adrian followed her with his eyes.
Several people around them probably knew it too.
Across the room, the Queen caught Claire's eye.
There was concern in her expression.
Adrian found Evelyn in a quiet corridor beyond the ballroom.
She had spilled wine on her gown and was waiting for an attendant to bring a cloth.
For several moments, Adrian stood at a distance.
He had not spoken to her since the night she married Nathaniel Brooks.
For months, he had forced himself not to ask questions.
Did she ever think about Adrian?
He had told himself that not knowing was better.
Now she was only a few yards away.
The woman he had loved since adolescence.
How was a person supposed to forget ten years simply because someone else had placed a ring on her finger?
The old familiarity pierced straight through him.
Almost immediately, Evelyn seemed to remember herself.
Adrian crossed the distance between them.
"You don't need to behave like a stranger with me."
She gave him a sad smile.
"If you wish, you may still call me what you used to."
But he could not bring himself to say the old pet name.
Instead, he looked at the elegant arrangement of her hair.
"You're married to Claire now. I'm married to Nathaniel. Of course things have changed."
"Claire has always cared for you very deeply. She'll treat you well. She always—"
Adrian immediately regretted the sharpness in his voice.
Evelyn gently removed her hand from his grasp.
Only then did Adrian realize he'd been holding it.
"Your wife is graceful, intelligent, and admired by everyone. You're well matched."
"I don't want anything except for you to be happy."
And for one terrible second, Adrian thought he saw tears.
Claire had stepped into the palace gardens to escape the heat.
She had no idea where Adrian had gone.
Her mouth curved in a humorless smile.
Just don't let anyone see you.
That was the only thing she asked of him anymore.
A voice came from behind her.
"Does the Duchess of Westbridge find royal receptions as tedious as I do?"
Claire put a little more distance between them.
"I only came outside because the ballroom was warm."
"I had hoped you came to admire the moon."
The moon was barely visible behind thin clouds.
Julian glanced upward as if he had only just remembered there was a sky above him.
"Then I suppose your poetry will have to wait."
"If the moon refuses to cooperate, I'll simply wait until sunrise and write about the sun."
Then, against her better judgment, laughed softly.
"Most poets would wait several nights for the perfect full moon."
"Then most poets have too much patience."
Claire suddenly remembered that they were alone.
A palace full of people who survived on gossip.
"We seem to have a habit of meeting unexpectedly."
"And please stop calling me 'the ambassador.' It makes me sound fifty."
He stepped back, maintaining a perfectly respectful distance.
"Then allow me to introduce myself properly."
Claire had the uncomfortable suspicion that refusing him would somehow be more awkward than accepting.

sections.title: Chapter Ten
paragraphs: Claire did not remain in the garden.
Julian's attention unsettled her in a way she wasn't accustomed to.
Perhaps it was simply because she had spent so little time alone with men who were not relatives.
Perhaps it was the way he looked at her.
As though he were actually interested in whatever she might say next.
Claire excused herself and returned toward the ballroom.
Then she reached the covered corridor.
Evelyn's face was buried against Adrian's chest. Her eyes were closed, her cheeks flushed, and her shoulders trembled as though she had been crying.
Several palace attendants stood nearby with their heads lowered, doing their best to pretend they could not see.
Claire's fingers closed around the fabric of her gown.
Before she had time to reconsider, she walked toward them.
For the first time Claire could remember, he looked caught.
She did not look at him.
"You appear to have had too much wine. Perhaps you should return to your husband before you embarrass yourself further."
Evelyn wiped her eyes and left without another word.
Not even the smallest acknowledgment of what had just happened.
Then she turned toward the palace attendants.
"His Grace has also had too much to drink."
"I trust none of you will be careless enough to turn a private mistake into public entertainment."
Only then did Claire look at Adrian.
For several seconds, guilt showed clearly on his face.
Then, as so often happened with Adrian, guilt became defensiveness.
"You behaved as though you'd caught us committing some great betrayal."
Some part of Adrian knew it.
She simply stood there in her immaculate blue gown, posture perfect, expression controlled.
"Whatever happened," Claire said, "should never have happened where others could see."

"We are at a royal reception. The Crown Prince's supporters are here. Foreign representatives are here. Half the aristocracy is here. If you wish to destroy your own reputation, at least don't do it quite so publicly."
"The perfect Duchess correcting everyone around her."
"You got your title because of House Ashford. Don't mistake that for the right to govern me."
The words hit exactly where he'd intended.
For the first time, Claire's expression cracked.
And in that ugly instant, some part of him felt victorious.
He hated how impossible she was to read.
He hated that he could hurt her and she refused to show him the wound.
"You forced your way into this marriage through your family. Surely you didn't also expect me to become some devoted husband simply because you decided you wanted one."
"We exchanged vows before the entire kingdom."
"And care for me, as I have tried to care for you."
It seemed to cost her something enormous to say those words.
Claire turned away before he could answer.
Her steps were controlled at first.
Behind her, she heard Adrian laugh once.
The sound followed her all the way back into the ballroom.
And suddenly Claire remembered their wedding night.
The way he'd looked at her then.
She did not remember returning to her seat.
The Queen had already left, pleading illness.
The king looked exhausted and flushed with wine and soon departed as well.
Adrian never returned to sit beside her.
Claire spent the rest of the evening alone.

sections.title: Chapter Eleven
paragraphs: Whatever fragile peace had grown between them vanished after the Spring Assembly.
Adrian and Claire returned to silence.
The weeks before the reception now seemed almost imaginary.
The conversations that had nearly begun to feel easy.
The military appointment Adrian had wanted eventually went to one of his younger brothers.
Privately, the political situation became increasingly tense.
Adrian returned home later each night.
Sometimes he did not return at all.
Westbridge House became enormous and quiet.
Claire spent most of her time with Anna and Lily.
By now, Lily understood far more about Claire's marriage than she had when she first arrived.
She was too intelligent not to.
But she never offered empty reassurance.
Several weeks later, Claire's carriage nearly overturned in a crowded street.
A drunken man stumbled in front of the horses.
The carriage lurched violently to one side.
Then came a sharp whistle from outside.
Claire steadied herself against the carriage wall.
Outside, the driver began speaking to someone.
A familiar man stood beside the carriage.
"Thank you. That could have become quite dangerous."
"A frightened horse is usually more frightened than dangerous."
"I'll send something to the Arden delegation as thanks."
"There's an excellent restaurant around the corner."
"And through a tragic failure of planning, I seem to have left my money behind."
Claiming he could not afford lunch.
It was the worst excuse she had ever heard.
"You planned that sentence before you approached the carriage, didn't you?"
And somehow, twenty minutes later, Claire found herself sitting across from the second prince of Arden in a private dining room at one of the capital's finest restaurants.
Quite generously, considering he was supposedly penniless.
Once the servants withdrew, he looked at Claire.
"I haven't seen you since the Spring Assembly."
Claire resisted the urge to point out that they were not supposed to see one another regularly.
Claire became increasingly aware of it.
Claire realized, with horror, that she had been looking at his eyes again.
"I've never seen eyes that color before."
"The color attracts attention because it's beautiful."
The words left her mouth before she could stop them.
Claire immediately wished she could take the sentence back.
"But if we're discussing eyes, I think yours are prettier."
For several minutes she believed the conversation had moved on.
"I've heard that one of the most accomplished women in the capital is an exceptional painter."
"I've been hoping to acquire a painting of horses before I return to Arden."
"You want me to recommend an artist?"
"I was hoping you might know one personally."
She had not painted seriously in years.
But Julian looked at her with such obvious amusement that her refusal somehow disappeared before it reached her mouth.
By the time she returned home that evening, she had agreed to paint him a picture.
She still wasn't entirely certain how.

sections.title: Chapter Twelve
paragraphs: Claire decided she needed her old paintings from Ashford Hall.
Only then did she realize something strange.
She had not returned home once since her wedding.
There was no custom requiring newly married daughters to visit their parents immediately, and noblewomen were often expected to establish themselves firmly in their husbands' households.
Claire sent word to Adrian's study telling him she intended to spend a day with her parents.
The moment Claire entered Ashford Hall, she nearly cried.
The same sitting room where her mother used to correct her embroidery.
The same smell of polished wood and old books.
There was more gray at his temples.
Her mother looked much the same.
Both of them were delighted to see her.
Her mother held Claire's face between her hands.
"Running a household isn't quite as easy as I imagined."
But his gaze remained on his daughter's face.
"At the military academy," her mother replied.
That answer made the sadness worse.
His voice was firm but not unkind.
"Now that you are Duchess of Westbridge, you must fulfill the responsibilities that come with it."
Her gaze drifted through the window.
Begging her father to arrange her marriage to Adrian.
At the time, Adrian was only beginning to emerge as a political rival to the Crown Prince.
The Crown Prince's faction wanted him destroyed before his influence grew.
Claire's eldest brother accidentally learned of a plot intended to disgrace Adrian permanently.
"Ask the king to marry me to him."
General Ashford had stared at her as though she'd gone mad.
"You want to throw away your entire life for a man who doesn't love you?"
"If I marry him, the Crown Prince will hesitate."
"Because people will assume House Ashford stands behind Adrian."
"I'm not asking you to choose a prince."
"Only that other people believe you might."
If Adrian married General Ashford's daughter, no enemy could know for certain where House Ashford stood.
Attacking him would suddenly become dangerous.
That did not make him happier.
"You want to use yourself as a shield."
"You think because he saved you once as a child, you owe him your entire future?"
When he returned, he looked older.
She never told him that gratitude was only part of it.
She had loved Adrian for years.
From the boy who rescued her in a marketplace to the prince who grew into a man she could never stop watching.
She knew he had once promised himself he would marry Evelyn.
But some selfish, deeply buried part of Claire had wondered—
What if she stopped standing behind everyone else and reached for something she wanted?
Maybe she loved Adrian too much.
Maybe she simply could not bear the thought of living the rest of her life knowing she had never even tried.
At the time, she could no longer tell the difference.
"I don't want you to spend the rest of your life regretting this."
Now, sitting in her childhood home almost a year later, she wondered if that answer had been a promise—
Her father studied her for a long moment.
"I only came because I need some of my old paintings."

sections.title: Chapter Thirteen
paragraphs: Claire sat before a blank canvas for nearly an entire afternoon.
Eventually, the light began to fade.
"I'm not very hungry tonight. Something light will be enough."
Before she could leave, the door opened.
She hadn't seen him properly in days.
For several seconds, he said nothing.
Rumors had been spreading through the capital for weeks.
Since the Spring Assembly, His Majesty had suffered repeated episodes of weakness. Physicians came and went from the palace at all hours.
No treatment seemed to help for long.
But the king's second son, once considered politically indifferent, had begun quietly gathering allies.
Every minister was choosing where to stand.
Claire understood the rest without being told.
If the king died tomorrow, the Crown Prince would inherit the throne.
Adrian had no legal path around that.
Not unless the king removed his heir first.
And if Adrian still wanted the crown—
there was only one path left.
Then Claire noticed something strange about the way he was watching her.
Yet whatever words he had prepared seemed unwilling to come.
But even House Ashford might not be enough.
Not against the Crown Prince's faction.
And Adrian had recently found one.
A man with pale eyes and an easy smile.
Julian Arden had made him an offer.
Adrian had thought about it for days.
Now, sitting in Claire's room, he found himself unable to repeat it.
Because Claire was looking at him.
And for the first time, the bargain sounded as ugly as it actually was.
He told himself the same thing he'd told himself whenever guilt became inconvenient.
Claire had forced him into this marriage.
She had used her family to change the course of his life.
She had never cared what he wanted.
Because otherwise he would have to admit what he was about to do.
He spoke quickly, before his courage failed.
"I need you to go to Arden."
Adrian continued before she could interrupt.
"When the succession happens, Arden is willing to support me."
That silence told her more than words could have.
A strange emptiness spread through her.
Perhaps more than she herself ever had.
Claire looked at him for a very long time.
For one foolish instant, the word almost hurt more than a command would have.
"Julian can give me what I need."
For years, she had wondered how much of herself she could give Adrian before there was nothing left.
That night, for the first time, she began to suspect she was close to finding out.

sections.title: Chapter Fourteen
paragraphs: For a long moment, Claire said nothing.
Then she looked at Adrian and asked quietly:
The words nearly destroyed every argument he had spent days building inside his own head.
Adrian could not meet her eyes.
Because even he understood what he had become.
A man willing to bargain with his own wife for power.
Arden would support Adrian's claim to the throne if Claire went with him.
Now he sat before Claire, unable to look at her because he was terrified of what he might find in her expression.
Instead, after a long silence, Claire said:
"The moment everything is settled, I'll bring you home."
Adrian leaned forward, desperate now to make the decision sound temporary.
"I'll never forget what you're doing for me."
"When you return, I'll treat you well."
Something almost pleading entered his voice.
"I swear it. I'll spend the rest of my life making this up to you."
Claire spoke before he could touch her.
"You were already supposed to treat me well."
"You were already supposed to spend your life not betraying me."
That was what made it unbearable.
A moment later, he stood and left the room with all the dignity of a man fleeing from himself.
Claire had very little time to prepare.
She told Anna only that she needed to leave the capital for a while.
"Don't change anything," Claire instructed her. "Keep the household running exactly as usual."
Claire closed the small case in front of her.
Several hours after Adrian left her room, someone tapped quietly on the window.
She left through the rear entrance in an ordinary covered coach.
At some point during the journey, she noticed an unfamiliar perfume in the carriage.
Then exhaustion overtook her with unnatural speed.
When Claire opened her eyes again, the capital was already far behind.
And sitting opposite her, reading as though this were the most ordinary journey in the world, was Julian Arden.
She did not take the glass.
She had no idea what awaited her.
Claire gave him a cold look.
"Forgive me for not trusting the man who arranged to take another man's wife across an international border."
Perhaps she was too tired to remain graceful.
Perhaps she had simply run out of reasons to pretend.
"I thought you might eventually consider it."
"Everyone in Valeria believes Adrian and I have a respectable marriage."
"Then why did your respectable husband give you away?"
"Perhaps you should ask yourself what you offered him."
"A thing to be traded between ambitious men."
After several minutes, Julian spoke again.
For just a moment, something complicated appeared in his pale eyes.
"You'll have your own residence. Servants. Privacy."
"And I will never touch you without your consent."
That made Claire look at him.
Then asked the question that had been following her since Adrian first mentioned the bargain.
But once again, he did not answer.

sections.title: Chapter Fifteen
paragraphs: That was almost more confusing than if he hadn't.
Claire was given a beautiful residence on the outskirts of Arden's capital.
It was secluded but not unpleasant.
The servants were efficient, discreet, and respectful. They did not question her. They did not gossip.
Claire was not expected to manage the household.
She was not required to attend court.
She did not have to entertain anyone.
For the first time in years, no one seemed to need anything from her.
A box of sweets from a famous bakery.
Tiny curiosities Claire had never seen in Valeria.
She repeatedly told him it wasn't necessary.
And, exactly as promised, Julian never crossed a boundary.
After two weeks, Claire became almost suspicious of how comfortable she was.
Had Adrian not effectively sold her into a foreign arrangement, she might have mistaken the entire situation for a holiday.
She was allowed everywhere within the estate.
The only restriction was that she could not leave unescorted.
Claire asked what explanation had been given for her disappearance back home.
She asked whether her family was safe.
That didn't mean she forgave him.
He was still a man who had demanded another man's wife as part of a political bargain.
Claire reminded herself of that frequently.
Then, one cold evening, she found herself sitting beneath a bare flowering tree in the courtyard.
Julian had somehow learned she liked blossoms and arranged for one to be planted there.
Claire stared up through the empty branches.
Once, she had loved spring flowers because they reminded her of Adrian.
Of the childhood gift he had given her.
Of the birthday he had insisted wasn't cursed.
Now they reminded her of her wedding.
Of the moment everything between them had begun to rot.
She wasn't sure she liked them anymore.
Julian took the seat across from her.
"I've told you that you don't need to be so formal."
"Good manners don't disappear simply because I'm angry with you."
Claire poured him a little spiced wine.
"You can't force something to bloom because you're impatient."
Claire had stopped punishing him with silence.
Not because she had forgiven him.
Because Adrian had been the one who agreed to give her away.
Julian could not have made that bargain alone.
Two hands were required to complete a transaction.
And one of them had belonged to her husband.
"You don't know whether I poisoned it."
Claire laughed softly and shook her head.
"Killing you would only leave me with a corpse and a murder charge."
Claire poured herself half a glass.
"Anna used to say I made this well."
The fewer people who understood the truth, the safer they were.
For a while, both sat in silence.
"Adrian is still important to you, isn't he?"
"The more I think about the past, the less certain I am what I actually felt."
"Perhaps I loved the version of myself who believed he might someday choose me."
"He saved me when I was a child."
"And later, when I felt as though something about me was cursed, he was the first person who told me it wasn't."
Her fingers tightened slightly around the glass.
"For years, I held onto those moments."
Claire felt something loosen inside her as she said them.
"I may have forced something that should never have been forced."
"But whatever debt I imagined I owed him has been paid many times over."
Julian's mother had been a foreign dancer brought to Arden's king as part of a diplomatic delegation.
In the royal family, those eyes marked him immediately as different.
Illegitimate-looking, even though he was not.
Julian had spent childhood hearing people whisper about his mother whenever they looked at him.
"They reminded everyone where my mother came from."
When Julian was a child, the king sent him abroad as a political hostage during a tense negotiation.
But long enough for a young boy to understand exactly how expendable he was.
"My father chose me because losing me would have mattered least."
"Then, when I was at my lowest, someone spoke to me."
"I never let her see me properly."
"I thought she'd react like everyone else."
"But she didn't ask why I hid."
"She told me my eyes must be beautiful."
"She said unusual did not mean ugly."
"She promised to paint something for me."
Claire could not breathe for a moment.
He stood before she could speak.
Claire remained beneath the bare tree.
Her heart was pounding for reasons she could not explain.

sections.title: Chapter Sixteen
paragraphs: Life in Arden was strangely peaceful.
Listened to him complain about ministers.
Sometimes they ate together and talked until the candles burned low.
Claire gradually stopped thinking about Valeria every morning when she woke.
There was something clean about it.
The world became softer beneath it.
That evening, Claire wrapped herself in a fur-lined cloak and went into the courtyard.
A small lantern glowed on the stone table.
Behind her, warm light spilled from the house.
Snow settled on Claire's hair and shoulders.
She closed her eyes and tilted her face upward.
For the first time in years, she felt completely still.
